Pronounce has two distinct meanings. They look different on the surface, but as you'll see by the end, a single powerful idea runs through both of them.
Meaning 1: To say a word aloud — correctly and clearly

This is the meaning most people learn first. When you pronounce a word, you use your mouth, tongue, and lips to produce the sounds of that word. Every word in a language has a correct way of being spoken — a specific combination of sounds — and pronouncing it means producing those sounds accurately.

Examples:

  • "Can you pronounce the word 'colonel'?" → Can you say that word with the right sounds?
  • "She finds it hard to pronounce French words." → She struggles to make French sounds correctly.
  • "He pronounced every word slowly and clearly." → He said each word deliberately, with correct sounds.

Notice the difference between say and pronounce. "Say" is completely neutral — it just means words came out of your mouth. "Pronounce" carries the added sense of doing it correctly, carefully, or deliberately. When someone asks, "How do you pronounce this word?" they are asking about the correct sounds — not just any sounds.
Meaning 2: To officially declare something — formally and with authority

This is the deeper, more powerful meaning. When someone pronounces something in this sense, they make a formal, official, and usually final statement. This is not casual speech. It is a declaration made by someone with authority — a judge, a doctor, a priest, an expert — and it carries real weight. It often changes something in the real world the moment it is said.

Think of a gavel coming down in a courtroom. The statement is definitive. There is ceremony in it. It is not just an opinion — it is an official conclusion.

Examples:

  • "The judge pronounced the man guilty." → The judge officially and formally declared him guilty. His legal status changed at that moment.
  • "The doctor pronounced the patient dead." → The doctor officially declared that the person had died.
  • "The priest pronounced them husband and wife." → The priest officially declared them married. Their status in the world changed.
  • "The committee pronounced the building unsafe." → The committee formally declared it dangerous — triggering real consequences.

This meaning can also be used in a softer, less ceremonial way — when someone gives a confident, final-sounding judgment, even without official authority:

  • "He tasted the wine and pronounced it excellent." → He gave his definitive verdict: the wine was excellent.
  • "She pronounced herself satisfied with the result." → She declared, with finality, that she was happy.

Even in these casual uses, you can feel the sense of authority and finality. The person isn't just giving a passing thought — they are delivering a verdict.
The hidden thread connecting both meanings

Here is the key insight that makes this word click: both meanings are about making something real through the act of speaking out loud.

In Meaning 1, you make a word real and clear by saying it with the correct sounds.
In Meaning 2, you make a fact, judgment, or status real and official by declaring it aloud.

In both cases, the speaking itself is what gives the word its power. You are not just thinking something — you are speaking it in a way that counts.

In Meaning 1, pronounce is followed by a word, name, or sound:

  • Pronounce a word / a name / a letter / a sound
  • "She couldn't pronounce his last name."
  • "This letter is not pronounced in French." (Here, the word is used in the passive — the letter is not said aloud.)

In Meaning 2, pronounce is typically followed by a person or thing plus a description of their new status:

  • Pronounce someone guilty / innocent / dead / married
  • Pronounce something a success / a failure / safe / dangerous
  • "The president was pronounced fit for duty."
  • "They pronounced the mission a success."

You will also encounter the phrase "pronounce on" something, which means giving an authoritative judgment about something:

  • "The critic pronounced on the quality of the new film." → The critic gave a formal, expert opinion about it.

Versus "say": "Say" is plain and neutral. "Pronounce" always adds a layer — either correctness of sounds (Meaning 1) or formality and authority (Meaning 2).

Versus "declare": These are very close in Meaning 2, but pronounce feels more ceremonial and final. A judge pronounces a sentence — the word suggests a ritual moment of significance. "Declare" is more straightforward. You would declare your income on a tax form, but a priest pronounces you married at the climax of a wedding. The sense of ceremony and weight is stronger with pronounce.

Versus "announce": To announce is to tell people about something publicly — like announcing a winner at an awards show. To pronounce is to make something officially real — like a judge making a verdict official. Announcing informs; pronouncing often determines.

The verb pronounce always involves speaking out loud in a way that matters — either because you are saying a word correctly (its sounds are right), or because you are saying something officially (your words carry authority and finality). Whether it's a child learning to pronounce a difficult word, a judge pronouncing a verdict, or a doctor pronouncing someone dead, the word always carries a sense that the act of speaking is important and intentional — not casual, not accidental, not half-hearted.
